word:lxx:L700002.explanation: This word means 1 and is also the name of the letter alpha. word:lxx:L700275.explanation: This word is a proper name, referring to a person named “Adina” or “Athina.” It functions as a personal designation rather than a description of an action, quality, or object. word:lxx:L700381.explanation: This word means “ancient.” It is a noun used to refer to something associated with great age or the distant past. word:lxx:L700406.explanation: This adjective means perpetual: continuing without end or interruption. It describes something enduring rather than temporary or short-lived. word:lxx:L700550.explanation: This LXX proper name refers to an Akkaronite, rendered in the lexical gloss as “Akkarōnitēs” or “Akkaronitis.” It identifies a person or people associated with that name rather than describing an action, quality, or object. word:lxx:L700734.explanation: This noun means “shackle” or “chains”—something used to bind or restrain a person. It names a physical restraint rather than an action or inner feeling. word:lxx:L700741.explanation: This noun means “threshing floor,” the place where harvested grain was processed and separated from its husks. word:lxx:L700778.explanation: This is a proper name, rendered “Amasai” or “Amase.” It identifies a person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. word:lxx:L700815.explanation: This adjective describes something that cannot be transferred, changed, or revoked. word:lxx:L700859.explanation: Amori means “Amori,” functioning as a proper name rather than a general description or action. word:lxx:L700998.explanation: Sinless describes someone or something without sin. word:lxx:L701489.explanation: This Greek Old Testament verb means “cut off”: to remove something by cutting it away or separate it from what it was attached to. word:lxx:L701562.explanation: Aporrētos means forbidden, describing something not to be spoken.

word:lxx:L701603.explanation: This verb means “tear away”: to pull something off or separate it forcefully. It describes an action rather than a person, object, or quality. word:lxx:L701904.explanation: This noun means “irreverence,” referring to a lack of reverence or honor toward God. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage, but its central idea remains irreverence—conduct that does not show due honor.

word:lxx:L701948.explanation: This adjective means “not of iron.” It describes something by saying that iron is not its material or quality, rather than naming the object itself. word:lxx:L701971.explanation: This Greek LXX verb means “well-pleased,” expressing a favorable or satisfied response. word:lxx:L703227.explanation: This adjective means “at the angle,” describing something located at or associated with a corner or angled point. word:lxx:L703285.explanation: This LXX Greek noun means “money lent; loan.” It refers to money given to another person with the expectation that it will be repaid, rather than to a gift or ordinary possession. word:lxx:L703322.explanation: This word means “in the evening.” It is an adjective that describes something as belonging to or occurring during the evening part of the day. word:lxx:L703933.explanation: Hebraios means Hebrew. It identifies an individual Hebrew and can also refer to the Hebrews as a people.

word:lxx:L705799.explanation: Zabadia, also rendered Zavathia, is a personal name in the Greek Old Testament. word:lxx:L705957.explanation: Ela, also rendered Ila, is a personal name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. word:lxx:L706138.explanation: This word means “wonderful.” It describes something remarkable and deserving of amazement or admiration. word:lxx:L706174.explanation: This adjective describes something that is wished for or desired—something a person wants or regards as desirable. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears only twice, so its basic sense is clear even though its particular force in each verse depends on the surrounding passage. It occurs in 1 Samuel 15:22 and Malachi 3:12. The word functions as a describing term rather than naming an action or person.

word:lxx:L706273.explanation: This verb means “crush”: to press or break something down by force. It describes an action rather than a person, object, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs 10 times, including nine Old Testament occurrences and one in the deuterocanonical books. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on what is being crushed and the surrounding sentence.

word:lxx:L706310.explanation: This Greek LXX noun means “religion,” referring to the practice or expression of religious devotion. It names religion as a recognizable way of honoring and serving a deity, rather than describing a person, place, or isolated action. The word occurs four times in the deuterocanonical Greek writings represented here: twice in Wisdom and twice in 4 Maccabees. Its precise force in any one passage depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central meaning remains religion or religious practice. This word belongs to the Greek LXX corpus and should be understood within that corpus.

word:lxx:L706440.explanation: Iarmoth is a proper name in the Greek LXX, identifying someone or something named Iarmoth. Its exact referent—whether a person, place, or another named entity—cannot be determined from the lexical information alone, so the surrounding verse is needed for that distinction. This name occurs once in the LXX corpus, at Ezra 10:27. It is not a general description or action word, but a specific name.

word:lxx:L706505.explanation: Idouram, also rendered Ithuram, is a personal name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it identifies one individual and appears only once, in 1 Chronicles 18:10. Because names primarily identify people, its significance here is the person it names, not a general concept that can be applied elsewhere. The surrounding verse provides the specific context for that individual’s appearance.

word:lxx:L706549.explanation: This proper noun identifies a Jezreelite, also rendered “Iezrelitis.” It functions as a personal or identifying designation connected with the people or place named Jezreel. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs nine times across eight verses, appearing in 1 Kings and 2 Kings. Its references are concentrated in 1 Kings 20 and continue through 2 Kings 9. The word itself supplies a designation rather than describing an action, quality, or spiritual concept.

word:lxx:L706813.explanation: Isei, also rendered Isi, is a personal name rather than a descriptive word or action. In the Greek Septuagint, it appears twice, both times in 1 Chronicles. The name itself identifies a person, but the available information does not provide an additional meaning or description attached to it. Its precise significance in either passage must therefore be understood from the surrounding verse and family or historical context.

word:lxx:L706930.explanation: Iōnan is a proper name, rendered in the supplied lexical information as “Iōnan” or “Ionan.” It identifies a person rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament and related LXX corpus, it occurs nine times, eight of them in Jonah and once in 3 Maccabees. The name appears repeatedly throughout the account of Jonah, including Jonah 1:1, 1:7, 1:15, 2:1, 2:11, and 3:1. Its precise significance in any particular verse comes from the surrounding passage.

word:lxx:L707029.explanation: This adverb means “arm fully” or “equip,” describing an action carried out with complete preparation or weaponry. It tells how someone is equipped or made ready, rather than naming the person, object, or equipment itself. The word appears once in the Greek Old Testament corpus, in 3 Maccabees 5:23. Because the verse text and surrounding passage are not included here, its precise force in that sentence must be understood from the context. Its central idea remains thorough equipping or full arming.

word:lxx:L707065.explanation: This noun refers to a misadventure or failure—a situation in which an undertaking goes badly or a person experiences an unsuccessful outcome. It names the unfortunate result itself rather than describing an action. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX) corpus, it occurs once, in Wisdom 5:23. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its central sense is an adverse outcome or failure. [Source: Wisdom 5:23]

word:lxx:L707160.explanation: Karmelon is a place-name, rendered Carmel in the English text.

word:lxx:L707182.explanation: Karterōs means strongly. In its scriptural setting, it describes Noah’s ark bearing up against the waves.

word:lxx:L707216.explanation: This Greek LXX verb means “feed flocks upon,” describing the act of letting sheep or other flock animals feed on something. It functions as an action word rather than a name or description. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs three times, all within Exodus 22:4. The broader sense remains focused on providing or directing food for a flock, while the precise object being grazed depends on the sentence where the verb appears.

word:lxx:L707331.explanation: Katamēnios means menstrual, describing something related to menstruation.

word:lxx:L707344.explanation: The word means “goal” or “end”: it names the point toward which something reaches or the concluding point itself. As a noun, it refers to an outcome or endpoint rather than describing an action. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Psalm 18:7, so its wider range of use cannot be established from repeated appearances. Its precise force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage.

word:lxx:L707533.explanation: This noun means “dwelling” or “inhabiting”—the condition or act of living in a place. It points to residence or settled presence rather than movement through an area. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Psalm 106:36, so its precise force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage. The word’s central idea remains clear: making a place one’s dwelling or living there.

word:lxx:L707586.explanation: Kedēmōth, also rendered Kethimoth, is a proper name in the Greek Old Testament. It identifies a named place or person rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. The name occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, at Joshua 13:18. Without the surrounding verse text, its precise referent cannot be explained further here; however, the lexical meaning is the name itself, not a broader descriptive term.

word:lxx:L707735.explanation: Klimakteres means a round of a ladder.

word:lxx:L707779.explanation: This verb means “sleep” or “encamp,” describing lying down to rest or staying in a camp. In the Greek Old Testament, it is used for ordinary resting and for dwelling in a place, so its exact sense depends on the sentence. The word occurs eight times across eight verses, including passages from Leviticus, Deuteronomy, Psalms, Jeremiah, Zephaniah, and Song of Songs. It can therefore refer either to nighttime rest or to lodging and settlement.

word:lxx:L707797.explanation: This adjective means “slit-nosed,” describing someone whose nose has a cleft or narrow split. It is a physical description rather than a name for a person or an action. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Leviticus 21:18. The surrounding verse would be needed to explain how the description functions in that specific passage, but the word itself points plainly to the shape or condition of the nose.

word:lxx:L707872.explanation: This word means “tassel,” a hanging decorative or identifying element attached to clothing or fabric. It is a noun naming a physical object rather than an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs five times across four verses, appearing in Numbers, Deuteronomy, and Zechariah. Its precise significance in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its ordinary meaning remains a tassel or attached hanging piece.

word:lxx:L707890.explanation: Kreisson means better, describing one thing as preferable to another.

word:lxx:L707946.explanation: This verb means “act as pilot”: to perform the work of guiding or directing as a pilot. It describes someone carrying out a pilot’s role rather than merely possessing that position. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs three times, in Proverbs and Wisdom, including references in Proverbs 12:5, Wisdom 10:4, and Wisdom 14:6. Its precise force in any one passage depends on the surrounding verse and its subject.

word:lxx:L708103.explanation: This word means “hewn out,” describing something shaped by cutting or carving. It functions as an adjective or noun, identifying an object made by being cut from a material rather than left in its natural form. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in 2 Kings, at 2 Kings 12:13 and 2 Kings 22:6. Its basic meaning remains focused on the result of workmanship: something cut out, carved, or fashioned by human labor.

word:lxx:L708262.explanation: This word is a proper name, rendered “Loōmim” or “Loomim.” It functions as a name rather than a common word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs only once, in Genesis 25:3. The available form identifies the name itself, while the surrounding verse determines whom or what the name identifies in that passage. It should therefore be understood as a named designation, not expanded into an abstract meaning or translated as an ordinary descriptive term.

word:lxx:L708280.explanation: This adjective describes something that pays what is due. It refers to fulfilling an obligation or settling what is properly owed. The word therefore focuses on the payment or fulfillment itself, not on a person’s title or identity. In the Greek LXX material represented here, it occurs once, in Sirach 28:21. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording.

word:lxx:L708389.explanation: Mainomai means to rave or be mad.

word:lxx:L708419.explanation: This word means “patience”: the steady endurance that does not quickly give up or react harshly. It is a noun describing a quality a person may show while waiting, suffering, or dealing with difficulty. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek Jewish writings represented here, it occurs five times, across Proverbs, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Sirach, and 1 Maccabees. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

word:lxx:L708455.explanation: Mambre is a name used for both a place and a person.

word:lxx:L708576.explanation: This noun means “superficiality,” describing what lacks depth, substance, or lasting value. In the Greek Old Testament, it is used 54 times, especially in Ecclesiastes and Psalms. Its repeated use in Ecclesiastes fits language about the fleeting and insubstantial character of earthly life, while its appearances in Psalms show that the word can also describe what proves empty or unreliable before God. The surrounding verse determines exactly what is being called superficial, but the central idea remains something lacking true weight or enduring substance.

word:lxx:L708770.explanation: Mesoulam is a personal name, rendered Mesulam in English.

word:lxx:L708792.explanation: This Greek LXX verb means to follow closely after someone or to pursue them. It describes directed action: staying after a person in close pursuit rather than merely noticing or accompanying them. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 2 Maccabees 2:31. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its basic meaning remains the act of following closely or pursuing.

word:lxx:L708837.explanation: This Greek LXX noun means “participation” or “partnership”—sharing in something or having a part with others. It describes involvement or fellowship rather than merely observing from a distance. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 4 Maccabees 2:1. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea is taking part together in something shared.

word:lxx:L708918.explanation: This word means “little” and functions as an adverb, describing something as small in degree or amount. It expresses a limited extent rather than a large or complete measure. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 14:8. Its exact force in that passage depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central sense remains a small amount or limited degree.

word:lxx:L708921.explanation: This verb means “mimic”: to imitate or copy someone or something. It describes an action rather than a person, expressing the act of reproducing another’s manner or behavior. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs four times, in Wisdom and 4 Maccabees. Its basic sense remains straightforward, while the surrounding verse determines what is being imitated and why. The word’s identity and explicit definition support “mimic” as its central meaning.

word:lxx:L709027.explanation: This word means “little calf,” referring to a young cow or bull. It is a noun used in the Greek Old Testament for an animal, including calves presented in sacrificial settings and calves prepared as food. The word occurs 12 times in 12 Old Testament verses, from Genesis through Malachi. Its ordinary meaning remains specific and concrete: a young bovine animal, rather than a general word for livestock or sacrifice.

word:lxx:L709122.explanation: Naana is a proper name referring to a person named Naana. It is not presented here as a general description, action, or quality, but as an individual’s name. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs once, in 1 Chronicles 8:7. The name’s precise significance beyond identifying that person is not established by the available lexical definition, so it is best understood simply as the personal name Naana.

word:lxx:L709243.explanation: Neesthan is a proper name preserved as “Neesthan” in the Greek Old Testament. It is not a general word describing an action, quality, or object; its role is to identify a particular named entity. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, at 2 Kings 18:4. The name’s specific reference and significance must be understood from that passage’s actual wording and surrounding context.

word:lxx:L709311.explanation: This Greek LXX noun means “conquest”—the gaining of victory over an opposing person, people, or power. It points to the achieved triumph itself rather than describing the act of fighting as a process. The word occurs three times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, appearing once in 2 Samuel and twice in the Maccabean books. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

word:lxx:L709328.explanation: This Greek LXX noun means “perception,” referring to the mind’s awareness or grasp of something. It names an inner act of recognizing or taking in what is presented, rather than an outward action. The word occurs twice in the deuterocanonical Greek writings, in Baruch and 3 Maccabees. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and sentence. word:lxx:L709445.explanation: Ogotholia is a proper name preserved in the Greek Old Testament. It identifies a particular named entity, but the available lexical information does not specify whether that entity is a person, place, or something else. This name occurs once in the Greek Old Testament corpus, at 1 Chronicles 8:26. Its precise referent must therefore be understood from that passage’s surrounding text rather than from the name alone.

word:lxx:L709500.explanation: This Greek LXX noun means “cell,” referring to a confined or enclosed space. It identifies a particular kind of room or compartment rather than an action or quality. The word occurs twice in the Greek LXX corpus, once in Ezekiel and once in Wisdom. Its precise significance in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and its description of the space. The basic meaning remains a cell: an enclosed place set apart for a specific purpose.

word:lxx:L709672.explanation: Ontōs means really or truly, as in a statement rendered “Truly,” where it emphasizes that what is said is genuinely so.

word:lxx:L709690.explanation: This noun means “little awl,” a small pointed tool used for piercing or making a hole. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs only twice, in Exodus 21:6 and Deuteronomy 15:17. Its ordinary meaning identifies the physical instrument itself rather than an action, person, or quality. The word therefore refers to a specific hand tool, with the surrounding verse determining how that tool is being used in its sentence.

word:lxx:L709746.explanation: This adverb means “uprightly” or “normally.” It describes how an action is performed or how something is regarded: in a right, proper, or ordinary manner. The word appears 16 times in the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical books, so its basic sense is consistent while the surrounding sentence determines whether it points to proper conduct or what is usual. It does not name a person or object; it qualifies an action, judgment, or description.

word:lxx:L709979.explanation: This adjective means “all-seeing”: it describes one who sees everything or is aware of all things. It presents comprehensive sight or awareness rather than limited human observation. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, the word occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 9:5. The reference identifies where it appears, but the surrounding verse text is needed to explain its particular force there. Its basic meaning remains a description of complete sight or awareness.

word:lxx:L709997.explanation: Paraballō means to cast along, as when something is let fall for another to gather. It can also mean to set against, as in putting one's body and life at risk.

word:lxx:L710115.explanation: This word means “mad”: it describes someone acting in a state of madness or lacking sound judgment. As a verb, it expresses becoming or behaving mad rather than naming a person or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Zechariah 7:11. That reference identifies its sole occurrence, while the word’s precise force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage.

word:lxx:L710159.explanation: This word describes a resident or foreigner—someone living in a place without being regarded as a native member of that community. It can refer to a person dwelling among another people or residing in a land that is not understood as his permanent homeland. As an adjective, it describes that status or condition. In the Greek Old Testament and related LXX writings, it occurs 23 times, showing repeated use for people living among others as non-natives.

word:lxx:L710252.explanation: “For mourning” or “mournful” describes something connected with grief and the outward expression of sorrow. As an adjective, the word characterizes a person, object, or appearance as suited to mourning rather than naming the act of mourning itself. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears twice, once in Exodus and once in 2 Samuel. Its central sense remains consistent: marked by grief or intended for a season of sorrow. The surrounding verse determines exactly what it describes in each passage.

word:lxx:L710326.explanation: This verb means to “burn round about,” describing burning that takes place around something rather than simply at one isolated point. Its basic sense focuses on the action itself and does not, by itself, explain the wider situation or purpose. In the Greek LXX corpus, it appears only once, at 4 Maccabees 16:3, so its precise force there depends on the verse and surrounding passage.

word:lxx:L710393.explanation: This Greek LXX noun refers to adornment or a robe—something worn as clothing or used to enhance appearance. Its central idea is an outward covering or decoration, rather than an action or inner quality. It occurs twice in the LXX corpus, once in Exodus and once in Sirach, showing its use for a tangible garment or adornment. The surrounding verse determines which aspect is emphasized.

word:lxx:L710414.explanation: This verb means “plant round about,” describing the act of setting plants around something or arranging them in a surrounding growth. It is an action word rather than a name or description of a person. In the Greek Septuagint corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 4 Maccabees 2:21. The precise force of the action in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea is planting in an encircling or surrounding arrangement.

word:lxx:L710458.explanation: This noun means “worker in clay,” referring to a person whose work involves shaping or handling clay. It identifies an occupation rather than an abstract quality or action. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, at Wisdom 15:7. Its basic meaning is therefore specific and concrete: a clay worker. The surrounding verse is needed to explain the word’s particular role in that passage.

word:lxx:L710461.explanation: This verb means to lame or maim—to cause someone or something to lose normal physical ability through injury. It describes an action rather than a person or condition, so its sentence role is to express what is done to another. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in 4 Maccabees 18:21. That reference identifies its location, while the surrounding verse text would be needed to explain the specific situation there.

word:lxx:L710520.explanation: This adjective means “numerous,” describing a group or collection that contains many individuals or things. It emphasizes quantity rather than identity, quality, or importance. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, in Deuteronomy 30:5 and 1 Maccabees 4:35. The surrounding words determine exactly what is numerous in each passage, but the central idea remains a large number or abundant company. Its use is straightforward: it adds the sense of many to the noun or subject it describes.

word:lxx:L710663.explanation: This verb means “pass the sea”—to travel across or through the sea. It describes an action rather than a person or object, showing what someone is doing. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Proverbs 30:19. Its central idea is movement across the sea; the precise force of that action in the verse depends on the surrounding passage. This is a Greek LXX word and should be understood within that Greek Old Testament setting.

word:lxx:L710784.explanation: This word means “forerunner”: someone who goes ahead of others. It can function as a noun for such a person or as an adjective describing someone or something that comes beforehand. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs three times, in Numbers, Isaiah, and Wisdom. Its basic idea is priority in movement or arrival—the one who precedes others. The surrounding verse determines what the forerunner is doing or why that precedence matters.

word:lxx:L710847.explanation: This Greek LXX verb means “address”: to speak to or call someone by a name or title. It describes the act of directing speech toward a person, rather than merely mentioning them. The word occurs seven times in the Greek LXX corpus, appearing once in Deuteronomy and six times in later deuterocanonical writings. Its precise force in any particular passage depends on whom the speaker addresses and why, but its central sense remains the direct act of addressing someone.

word:lxx:L710902.explanation: This verb means to predict—to declare or indicate something before it happens. It describes the act of foretelling an event or outcome, rather than merely noticing or describing what is already present. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in 4 Maccabees 15:19. Because the verse text and surrounding passage are not included here, the word’s precise force in that sentence must be understood from its context. Its central idea remains clear: giving advance notice of what is expected to happen.

word:lxx:L711008.explanation: Prophēteuō means to prophesy, speaking a message in God's name.

word:lxx:L711031.explanation: This verb means to “assume the first seat among,” describing someone taking the foremost place in a group. As a verb, it expresses an action rather than naming a person or object. In the Greek Old Testament (the LXX), it occurs once, in Esther 3:1. Because the verse text and surrounding passage are not included here, the word’s exact force in that occurrence must be understood from its context.

word:lxx:L711044.explanation: This word means “bring forth her first child”. It is a verb describing a first birth, and it can also refer to an animal calving for the first time. The word occurs three times in the Greek Old Testament, in 1 Samuel and Jeremiah. Its references concern the basic act of bringing forth a first offspring, while the precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

word:lxx:L711116.explanation: This Greek LXX verb means “trade” or “sell”: to exchange goods or property for something of value. It describes the act of offering something in commerce or transferring it to another person through a sale. The word occurs 16 times in the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical books, including passages involving food, land, servants, and merchandise. Its exact force in a particular verse depends on what is being exchanged and the surrounding sentence.

word:lxx:L711329.explanation: Saarēm; Saarim is a proper name, referring to a person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 8:8. Because no verse text or surrounding passage is provided here, the name itself gives the main meaning: it identifies an individual. Its precise identity and significance must be understood from the genealogy and context in that passage.

word:lxx:L711365.explanation: This word means “dragnet,” a large net used to gather fish. It is a noun referring to the fishing equipment itself, rather than the act of fishing or the people who fish. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs six times, including passages in Ecclesiastes, Isaiah, Ezekiel, and Habakkuk. Its normal meaning remains centered on a net drawn through the water to collect fish.

word:lxx:L711435.explanation: Samagoth is a proper name, referring to a specific person or place rather than expressing a general quality or action. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in Jeremiah 46:3. The available rendering preserves the name as “Samagoth,” matching the supplied meaning “Samagōth; Samagoth.” Because the surrounding verse text is not included here, the word’s precise role in that passage cannot be described further.

word:lxx:L711479.explanation: Samsaria is a proper name, referring to a particular person or place identified by that name rather than describing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in 1 Chronicles 8:26. Because it is a name, its ordinary meaning is its identifying designation; the surrounding verse is needed to determine exactly whom or what Samsaria identifies there.

word:lxx:L711497.explanation: Saou, also rendered Sau, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a person named in the Greek Old Testament tradition. This name occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, at 1 Chronicles 2:49. Because the verse text and surrounding passage are not included here, the name’s specific family or narrative role should be understood from that passage rather than inferred from the name itself.

word:lxx:L711707.explanation: Serran is a proper name, identifying a person rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Septuagint, it occurs once, in 2 Samuel 23:9. Since the available wording gives only the name itself and no surrounding verse text, its precise identity and role must be determined from that passage. The name should therefore be understood simply as “Serran,” a personal designation preserved in this one Old Testament occurrence.

word:lxx:L711800.explanation: Sirdatha is a proper name, given in the alternate form “Sirthatha.” It identifies a particular named entity rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs once, in 2 Chronicles 4:17. The available information establishes the name and its spelling forms, but the verse text is needed to determine exactly whom or what the name identifies in that passage.

word:lxx:L711945.explanation: This word means “of you” or “your.” It is a pronoun that connects something with the person or people being addressed, expressing possession or association. For example, it can identify something belonging to you or connected with you. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 5,764 times, so it is a common way to express this relationship across many kinds of sentences. Its exact English wording depends on the noun or phrase it accompanies, but its central idea remains connection with the person addressed.

word:lxx:L712009.explanation: This verb means “go to seed” or “seed,” referring to producing or scattering seed. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears twice, in Exodus 9:31 and Leviticus 12:2. Its basic sense belongs to the process of sowing or reproduction, depending on the sentence in which it occurs. The word therefore describes an action connected with seed, rather than naming the seed itself.

word:lxx:L712045.explanation: This Greek LXX verb means “drop” or “drip.” It describes liquid falling in drops or being released gradually, rather than pouring out all at once. As a verb, it expresses the action itself. This word occurs once in the Greek LXX, in Micah 2:11; the precise force of the word there depends on the surrounding verse and passage. Its basic idea remains the falling or dripping of liquid.

word:lxx:L712100.explanation: “Stoutly” means acting with firmness, strength, or determination. As an adverb, it describes how someone carries out an action rather than naming a person or thing. This Greek LXX word occurs once, in Habakkuk 2:6. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its central idea is resolute or forceful action. It should therefore be understood as describing the manner of an action: doing something stoutly.

word:lxx:L712272.explanation: This Greek LXX verb means “grieve altogether,” describing complete or deeply felt grief. It expresses the act of grieving rather than naming a person, object, or state. The word appears twice in the Greek Old Testament, once in Psalms and once in Isaiah, so its meaning is focused and specific rather than broadly varied across many passages. Its exact force in either verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea remains a full experience or expression of grief.

word:lxx:L712290.explanation: This Greek LXX verb means to “feed with” or “graze with,” describing animals sharing pasture or feeding alongside one another. It expresses joint feeding rather than merely eating, so the word focuses on creatures being together as they graze. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Isaiah 11:6, and its precise force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage. The word is therefore a concrete term for animals feeding together, with the shared setting included in its meaning.

word:lxx:L712346.explanation: “Fellow-drinker” or “boon-companion” describes a person who drinks with someone and is regarded as a companion in that setting. As a noun, the word identifies the person rather than the act of drinking. Its central idea is companionship joined to shared drinking, while the surrounding passage determines the particular tone or relationship intended. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, at 3 Maccabees 2:25.

word:lxx:L712485.explanation: This adjective describes something covered, darkened, or obscured by clouds—“clouded over; cloudy.” It portrays a sky or scene whose clarity is hidden beneath cloud cover, rather than something bright and clear. In the Greek Old Testament, this word occurs once, at Deuteronomy 33:28. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding verse text, but its ordinary meaning remains a description of cloudy or overcast conditions.

word:lxx:L712522.explanation: This Greek LXX noun means “ruin” or “crushing”—the condition or result of being broken down, overwhelmed, or brought to destruction. It describes severe damage or collapse rather than a person or action by itself. The word occurs five times in the Greek Old Testament, appearing once each in 2 Samuel, Jeremiah, Amos, Micah, and Zephaniah. Its precise force in any particular passage comes from the surrounding verse, but its central idea remains ruin or crushing.

word:lxx:L712643.explanation: This Greek LXX verb means “heap”: to gather or pile things together into a heap. It describes an action rather than a person or object, so its sentence role is to express the piling or accumulating of something. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in Proverbs 32:22.
